Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Law 10/2010 of 28 April on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, especially Articles 3, 4 and 7; Royal Decree 304/2014 of 5 May approving the implementing regulation of Law 10/2010; Royal Decree 609/2023 of 11 July establishing the Central Register of Beneficial Ownership (Registro Central de Titularidades Reales, RCTIR); Royal Decree-law 7/2021 of 27 April, as amended, concerning the transposition of EU beneficial-ownership and AML requirements; applicable EU Directive (EU) 2015/849, as amended. Companies must identify, verify, retain and provide beneficial-owner information. The primary ownership test is direct or indirect ownership of more than 25 percent of capital or voting rights, or control by other means; if no natural person is identified, the senior managing official fallback applies.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A Spanish SL must have a registered office in Spain under the Companies Act, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010, especially Articles 9 and 10. A virtual office may be used for registered-office and correspondence purposes if the provider lawfully permits its address to be used, accepts official notices and maintains document-delivery controls. It is not sufficient where the address is fictitious, inaccessible, unrelated to management or used to conceal the actual place of effective management. For ESG, carbon-accounting and advisory services, no general sector license is ordinarily required, but the company must not market its work as a statutory financial audit or accredited greenhouse-gas verification unless separately qualified and accredited under applicable Spanish, EU or sector-specific rules. Substance should include documented management, client files, accounting, AML controls, data protection compliance, tax records and adequate personnel or contractors.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central (name certification); Registro Mercantil Provincial of the registered-office province (final registration).

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July approving the consolidated text of the Capital Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital, LSC), Articles 20-22 (formation deed), 28 (minimum capital), 58-59 (registered office), 133 (corporate governance provisions), 196-204 (administrators); complemented by Royal Decree 1784/1996 (Commercial Registry Regulations).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura de Constitución (public deed of incorporation) executed before a Spanish notary and inscribed in the Registro Mercantil, followed by issuance of the definitive CIF/NIF by the Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT).

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 40 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

The SL minimum share capital is EUR 3,000 (LSC Art. 4), fully subscribed and fully paid at execution of the deed; payment is evidenced by a bank certificate of deposit (certificado de abono) dated within two months of the deed, or by notarized cash delivery; no escrow account is statutorily required; Spain charges no flat state formation fee, but notarial tariffs, registry tariffs and 1% stamp duty (Actos Jurídicos Documentados) on the capital value apply.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety: fire-extinguishing equipment and emergency lighting certified per CTE-DBSI and RIPCI (RD 513/2017), with periodic inspections; structure: CTE-SE compliance for any fit-out or heavy filing loads; occupation: valid lease and municipal occupancy certificate; workplace: Ley 31/1995 risk-prevention plan, first-aid kit, signage and evacuation drills for employees.

Paid-in capital rule: The SL minimum share capital is EUR 3,000 (LSC Art. 4), fully subscribed and fully paid at execution of the deed; payment is evidenced by a bank certificate of deposit (certificado de abono) dated within two months of the deed, or by notarized cash delivery; no escrow account is statutorily required; Spain charges no flat state formation fee, but notarial tariffs, registry tariffs and 1% stamp duty (Actos Jurídicos Documentados) on the capital value apply.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION. By invited general meeting of the founding members of [COMPANY NAME], S.L., unanimously, the following is resolved: (1) SHARE SUBSCRIPTION AND CAPITAL: The share capital of EUR 3,000, divided into 3,000 equal participaciones, is fully subscribed and paid in as evidenced by the bank certificate of deposit attached as Exhibit A; the participaciones are allotted among the founding members in accordance with the Articles of Association. (2) REGISTERED OFFICE: The registered office is fixed at [Premises Address], [City], Spain, for all legal, fiscal and corporate purposes. (3) APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS: [Full Name] is appointed Sole Administrator, with full powers under the Law. Approved and executed this [date].
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Exempted / Not Required

No sectoral industrial license is mandated for ISIC 7020 consultancy; the municipal Ayuntamiento supervises premises and activity licensing, while the Dirección General de Industria y de la Pyme (Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism) intervenes only for industrial-scale projects.

Category: Declaración Responsable de Inicio de Actividad / Licencia de Apertura (municipal operating clearance for non-industrial office premises); no specific regulated operating permit is required for ESG carbon auditing and offset brokerage.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT); online portal: sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

A Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada incorporated in Spain obtains its NIF (formerly CIF) from AEAT upon submission of Modelo 036/037, generally through its registered office or legal representative. Non-resident entities that wish to carry out taxable activities in Spain without a permanent establishment must file Modelo 030 or 036 to obtain a NIF-N before the first taxable transaction, providing apostilled/legalized articles of incorporation, appointment of a person with legal representation in Spain, and a certified copy of the representative's or director's NIE/passport. VAT registration is integrated into the same Modelo 036 filing; no separate pre-registration approval is required.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada incorporated in Spain obtains its NIF (formerly CIF) from AEAT upon submission of Modelo 036/037, generally through its registered office or legal representative. Non-resident entities that wish to carry out taxable activities in Spain without a permanent establishment must file Modelo 030 or 036 to obtain a NIF-N before the first taxable transaction, providing apostilled/legalized articles of incorporation, appointment of a person with legal representation in Spain, and a certified copy of the representative's or director's NIE/passport. VAT registration is integrated into the same Modelo 036 filing; no separate pre-registration approval is required.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain does not operate a check-the-box system. An SL is mandatorily subject to entity-level taxation under the Impuesto sobre Sociedades, with a general 25% rate and a reduced 15% rate for qualifying newly-created entities. No hybrid mismatch election is available for the SL itself; the only statutory transparency/elective schemes are temporary joint ventures (UTE), Spanish economic interest groupings (AIE/SEC) and consolidation elections, none of which alter the SL's separate corporate tax identity. Hybrid mismatch rules transposing ATAD apply automatically and cannot be opted out of.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general VAT registration threshold in EUR: any economic activity carried out in Spain requires filing Modelo 036 and obtaining a Spanish VAT number before operations begin. For intra-EU distance sales and certain cross-border digital services, the simplified EUR 10,000 annual threshold applies to non-established EU suppliers under the OSS regime, but a Spanish fixed establishment or any local supply triggers mandatory registration regardless of turnover.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Zero-rated VAT (0%) applies to exports of goods physically departing from Spain/EU territory, and to certain international services such as transport, loading and ancillary services, intra-community B2B supplies and financial services. For the SL's ESG carbon accounting audit and advisory services, exports of consulting services to a non-resident business recipient are outside the scope of Spanish VAT under article 70 LIVA if the recipient is established in a third country and the effective use and enjoyment occurs abroad; the SL must retain the client's foreign VAT ID or business registration evidence and the service contract. For physical exports, the exporter must demonstrate that the goods left the EU within the legally required period (generally within 3 months) and hold documentary evidence of export.

  • Customs Export Declaration (DUA/SAD — Documento Único Administrativo) validated by Spanish/European Customs with an export exit reference
  • Bill of Lading, airway bill or CMR transport document evidencing physical departure of goods from the EU
  • Inward Remittance Certificate or SWIFT/MATCH bank statement evidencing settlement of export proceeds
  • Commercial invoice with Incoterms and export movement reference
  • Exporter's VAT registration certificate and valid EORI number
  • Supporting documents for B2B service exports such as signed contract, ESG audit workpaper and recipient's tax identification certificate

Taxpayers with annual turnover exceeding EUR 6,010,121.40 and those in mandatory VAT groups must use the SII (Suministro Inmediato de Información), submitting invoice records to AEAT via web services/API in near real time, generally within 4 business days. General B2B e-invoicing will become mandatory once the implementing regulation under Ley 18/2022 'Crea y Crece' is enacted; in Basque Country and Navarre, the TicketBAI regime mandates QR-signed digital invoices and real-time fiscal reporting. Spain does not maintain a national central fiscal clearance server, but AEAT may cross-check invoice data and require electronic files in Facturae/XML format during audit procedures.

AEAT may reverse zero-rating with retrospective effect if the exporter fails to retain adequate proof of export or if the documentary chain is false. Reversal triggers VAT at 21% plus statutory late-payment interest. Penalties under articles 198 and 201 LGT range from 50% to 150% of the affected amount; serious infringement involving fraudulent or materially false documentation carries a 150% penalty. Where the defrauded VAT exceeds EUR 120,000, criminal tax-fraud prosecution under the Spanish Penal Code may be brought, with possible imprisonment and fines. Failure to repatriate export proceeds within the applicable exchange-control period may also result in separate administrative sanctions and loss of zero-rating benefits.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro and has no general exchange controls. Current-account convertibility is unrestricted, subject to ordinary bank, sanctions, anti-money-laundering, tax, customs and payment-screening controls. Capital-account movements, including non-resident equity funding, intercompany loans, dividends, royalties, interest and liquidation proceeds, are generally transferable without prior central-bank approval. A Spanish SL may remit dividends or other distributions only after valid corporate approval, satisfaction of applicable Spanish company-law solvency and reserve requirements, payment or withholding of applicable taxes, and maintenance of adequate accounting evidence. Non-resident direct-investment reporting, foreign-investment declarations, statistical reporting and bank information requests may apply depending on transaction type, investor status, amount and sector. Dividend payments to non-residents may be subject to Spanish withholding tax, subject to domestic exemptions or an applicable tax treaty, including the Spain-EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive where all statutory conditions are met. Interest, royalties, service fees and related-party payments require arm's-length support, beneficial-owner evidence, transfer-pricing documentation and withholding-tax analysis. Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, high-risk counterparties, opaque ownership, virtual-asset exposure or unexplained third-party funding may be delayed or rejected.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no statutory export-proceeds surrender requirement, no mandatory conversion ratio and no general deadline requiring export receipts to be converted into euros or deposited with a Spanish bank. Export proceeds may remain in foreign-currency accounts or be received through foreign or Spanish payment institutions, subject to accounting, tax, customs, sanctions, AML and bank reporting requirements. The company should retain contracts, invoices, transport or service-delivery evidence, customs records where applicable, bank confirmations, reconciliation schedules and proof of beneficial ownership. Banks may impose contractual cut-off dates, request evidence of trade or services, apply internal conversion requirements, or report transactions under regulatory and statistical frameworks; these private compliance measures do not constitute a statutory surrender rule. Physical cross-border movement of cash or bearer negotiable instruments of EUR 10,000 or more is subject to EU and Spanish declaration requirements. Electronic transfers remain subject to payment-screening and applicable EU funds-transfer information rules.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), operating within the Eurosystem under the European Central Bank framework. Foreign-investment and balance-of-payments reporting is administered under Spanish legislation by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Enterprise, including its Directorate-General for International Trade and Investments.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium for payment operations and low-to-medium for full treasury banking. An EU-authorised electronic-money institution or payment institution may provide payment accounts, SEPA transfers, cards, foreign-exchange services and, where authorised, safeguarded client-money arrangements. It is not a bank and generally cannot accept deposits or provide a conventional capital escrow account unless the product and legal structure expressly support the required corporate formation process. Offshore digital EMIs without EU passporting, an applicable Spanish authorisation or a regulated EU establishment should not be used for Spanish share-capital funding, payroll, tax remittances or material operating liquidity. The SL must complete institutional KYB, beneficial-owner identification, source-of-funds checks, sanctions screening and transaction monitoring. Safeguarding, account-closure, geographic availability, settlement-bank dependency, fund-recovery and insolvency protections must be reviewed before material balances are placed with an EMI.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Non-resident ownership, nominee shareholders, layered holding companies or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Root cause: Non-resident ownership, nominee shareholders, layered holding companies or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Defense evidence: Current certificate of incorporation and good-standing evidence for every holding entity; constitutional documents; complete ownership chart to natural-person beneficial owners; shareholder registers; passports and residential-address evidence; director and signatory resolutions; beneficial-owner declaration; rationale for the ownership chain; and certified or apostilled documents with accepted translations.
Incoming capital from an account held by a shareholder, affiliate, director or unrelated third party rather than the disclosed investor.

Root cause: Incoming capital from an account held by a shareholder, affiliate, director or unrelated third party rather than the disclosed investor.

Defense evidence: Executed subscription or capital-increase agreement; shareholder resolution; bank evidence identifying the remitter; source-of-funds and source-of-wealth statement; audited or management accounts; loan agreement where relevant; intercompany funding resolution; beneficial-owner evidence; payment-purpose narrative; and reconciliation linking the transfer to the subscribed amount.
ESG, carbon-credit, offset-brokerage or environmental-commodity activity viewed as a higher-risk or insufficiently transparent payment sector.

Root cause: ESG, carbon-credit, offset-brokerage or environmental-commodity activity viewed as a higher-risk or insufficiently transparent payment sector.

Defense evidence: Detailed business plan; service descriptions; client and supplier profiles; standard engagement agreements; carbon-accounting methodology; verification or assurance-provider information; registry and project documentation for any credits; evidence that the company does not operate an unlicensed investment, payment, money-remittance or cryptoasset business; expected transaction flows; geographic risk matrix; sanctions-screening procedure; and sample invoices.
Expected cross-border flows inconsistent with a newly incorporated consultancy, including high-value transfers, Latin American exposure, rapid pass-through activity or substantial cash receipts.

Root cause: Expected cross-border flows inconsistent with a newly incorporated consultancy, including high-value transfers, Latin American exposure, rapid pass-through activity or substantial cash receipts.

Defense evidence: Twelve-month cash-flow forecast; transaction-volume and corridor schedule; projected countries, currencies and counterparties; signed or prospective contracts; invoice samples; tax registration evidence; staffing and premises information; treasury policy; segregation-of-duties matrix; explanation of payment timing; and documented approval controls for unusual transactions.
Foreign documents that are expired, unauthenticated, untranslated or inconsistent with Spanish corporate-register information.

Root cause: Foreign documents that are expired, unauthenticated, untranslated or inconsistent with Spanish corporate-register information.

Defense evidence: Recent registry extracts; apostille or legalisation where required; certified Spanish translations; certificate of incumbency; current powers of attorney; Spanish tax identification numbers; registered-office evidence; notarial copies where requested; and a document-control schedule showing issue dates and renewal dates.
Sanctions, politically exposed persons, adverse media, high-risk jurisdictions or unexplained exposure to cash, virtual assets or restricted goods.

Root cause: Sanctions, politically exposed persons, adverse media, high-risk jurisdictions or unexplained exposure to cash, virtual assets or restricted goods.

Defense evidence: Enhanced due-diligence memorandum; PEP and sanctions screening results; beneficial-owner wealth and income evidence; country-risk assessment; contractual purpose and end-use evidence; independent compliance review; transaction approval matrix; evidence of no prohibited counterparties; and escalation records for any false-positive screening result.
Related-party service fees, royalties, interest or management charges that could indicate profit diversion or tax evasion.

Root cause: Related-party service fees, royalties, interest or management charges that could indicate profit diversion or tax evasion.

Defense evidence: Intercompany agreements; transfer-pricing policy and local file where applicable; benchmarking; board approval; evidence of services actually performed; time records and deliverables; invoice calculations; withholding-tax analysis; treaty-residence and beneficial-owner certificates; and accounting and tax reconciliation.
Failure to demonstrate Spanish operational substance or mismatch between declared activity and account usage.

Root cause: Failure to demonstrate Spanish operational substance or mismatch between declared activity and account usage.

Defense evidence: Lease or registered-office agreement; employee or contractor information; management biographies; customer contracts; website and marketing materials; accounting records; tax registrations; expected payroll and supplier schedule; governing-body minutes; and evidence that payment activity matches the declared ESG advisory and carbon-accounting business.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Execute the capital contribution from an account held in the name of the disclosed shareholder or investor directly to the Spanish bank account designated for capital funding. Obtain the bank's capital-payment certificate or equivalent evidence, complete the required corporate resolution and capital-increase or formation documentation, and register the transaction with the Mercantile Registry where legally required. Use a clear payment reference such as share capital contribution, share premium contribution or shareholder loan, and do not mix legally distinct funding types. For shareholder loans, execute the loan agreement before payment and document maturity, interest, transfer-pricing treatment and repayment terms. Provide the receiving bank with investor identity, beneficial-owner information, source-of-funds evidence, subscription documents, expected amount, currency, purpose and originating-bank details. Use SWIFT cross-border transfer, SEPA Credit Transfer for euro payments within the relevant SEPA perimeter, or another regulated payment rail. Banks may request foreign-investment declarations, balance-of-payments information, statistical reporting and evidence of tax or corporate treatment; the applicable filing depends on the transaction and investor profile. Reconcile the bank statement, corporate ledger, shareholder register, registry filing and tax records. Avoid third-party remitters, split payments, unexplained cash, cryptoasset settlement and payments from sanctioned or high-risk jurisdictions.Use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant Credit Transfer for qualifying euro payments; SWIFT cross-border transfers for non-SEPA currencies or jurisdictions; and SWIFT MT103 or its ISO 20022 successor equivalent for documented customer-credit transfers. For higher-risk or documentary trade, use a commercial letter of credit, preferably an irrevocable and, where justified, confirmed documentary credit subject to UCP 600, with document presentation, sanctions screening and discrepancy controls. Documentary collections may use URC 522. Maintain contracts, purchase orders, invoices, bills of lading or equivalent transport evidence, certificates of origin, customs documentation, service-delivery evidence, beneficiary bank details and payment approvals. Screen counterparties, banks, vessels, goods, countries and beneficial owners against applicable EU, UN and Spanish sanctions. Apply segregation of duties, dual approval, beneficiary-account verification, payment-limit controls and post-payment reconciliation. For exports of services, retain engagement letters, deliverables and evidence of performance. For imported goods or carbon-related instruments, confirm the legal nature, registry, ownership, transferability, VAT and accounting treatment before payment. Do not use trade rails to disguise shareholder distributions, intercompany loans, capital movements or prohibited financial services.Deliverable FX forwards for identifiable forecast or committed commercial exposures, documented under appropriate bank or master trading documentation and supported by treasury-policy approvals.Non-deliverable forwards where the relevant currency is non-convertible or where cash settlement is legally and operationally appropriate. Confirm that the counterparty is authorised, the transaction is not speculative under internal policy, and applicable EMIR classification, reporting, margin and risk-mitigation obligations are addressed.Currency swaps and cross-currency swaps for documented recurring cash-flow or funding exposures, subject to counterparty credit limits, collateral terms, valuation controls, accounting treatment and applicable EMIR requirements.FX spot transactions for settlement and operational conversion, including conversion of customer receipts, payroll funding, tax payments and supplier obligations.Currency options, collars or option combinations only where permitted by the counterparty, appropriately disclosed, approved under the treasury policy and assessed for suitability, premium, contingent exposure, accounting and regulatory consequences.Intra-group netting or natural hedging through currency matching may be used where supported by genuine underlying flows, arm's-length documentation, transfer-pricing analysis and appropriate intercompany settlement controls. Speculative derivatives, undocumented back-to-back trades and hedges unrelated to genuine business exposure should be prohibited.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium for payment operations and low-to-medium for full treasury banking. An EU-authorised electronic-money institution or payment institution may provide payment accounts, SEPA transfers, cards, foreign-exchange services and, where authorised, safeguarded client-money arrangements. It is not a bank and generally cannot accept deposits or provide a conventional capital escrow account unless the product and legal structure expressly support the required corporate formation process. Offshore digital EMIs without EU passporting, an applicable Spanish authorisation or a regulated EU establishment should not be used for Spanish share-capital funding, payroll, tax remittances or material operating liquidity. The SL must complete institutional KYB, beneficial-owner identification, source-of-funds checks, sanctions screening and transaction monitoring. Safeguarding, account-closure, geographic availability, settlement-bank dependency, fund-recovery and insolvency protections must be reviewed before material balances are placed with an EMI.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax generally applies to dividends and other profit distributions paid by a Spanish company to non-residents, subject to domestic exemptions, European Union directives, tax treaties, beneficial-ownership requirements, and anti-abuse rules. A qualifying EU or European Economic Area parent may potentially obtain exemption under the Spanish implementation of the Parent-Subsidiary Directive, commonly requiring at least a 10% participation held for the statutory minimum period and satisfaction of anti-abuse and subject-to-tax conditions.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within the first 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the ordinary filing window is 1 to 25 July of the following year, subject to the statutory electronic filing rules and next-business-day adjustments where applicable.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally filed during the first 20 calendar days of April, October, and December. Where the taxpayer is required to use the alternative taxable-base method, the installments are calculated using the relevant current-year tax-base information rather than only the prior return liability.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally filed in the month following the ten-month period after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the ordinary deadline is November of the following year.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain generally requires transfer-pricing documentation for controlled transactions, with simplified documentation potentially available for entities or groups below the applicable EUR 45 million net-turnover threshold. Modelo 232 reporting is generally triggered for transactions of the same type and valuation method exceeding EUR 250,000 in aggregate with the same related counterparty, transactions with non-cooperative jurisdictions exceeding EUR 100,000 in the relevant categories, or where the aggregate controlled transactions exceed 50% of the entity's turnover, subject to statutory details and exclusions. The master file is generally relevant to Spanish entities forming part of a multinational group, while the local file covers the Spanish taxpayer and its material controlled transactions.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no single standalone regime titled Economic Substance Regulations equivalent to certain offshore jurisdictions. Economic substance is nevertheless enforced through Spanish transfer-pricing rules, beneficial-ownership requirements, the principal-purpose and anti-abuse rules, general anti-avoidance doctrine, controlled foreign company rules, hybrid-mismatch rules, interest-limitation rules, EU anti-abuse legislation, and treaty provisions. A Spanish SL receiving management fees, royalties, financing income, or service income should maintain genuine Spanish personnel or outsourced operational capacity, decision-making, premises or operational infrastructure appropriate to the business, commercial risk assumption, contemporaneous records, and evidence of actual services and value creation. Carbon credits and offset-brokerage transactions require traceable title, delivery, registry records, pricing support, and evidence that the Spanish entity performs the claimed functions.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate Income Tax evasion and fraudulent tax reporting

Statutory sanction: Administrative penalties may generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax, plus tax, interest, and collection costs. Tax fraud may become a criminal offense when the defrauded tax exceeds EUR 120,000 for the relevant tax period, generally punishable by imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine of one to six times the amount defrauded, with aggravated ranges for qualified cases.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may face civil and administrative liability where they caused, facilitated, or failed to prevent the breach. Criminal liability may include imprisonment, fines, disqualification, restitution, and asset measures. Corporate separateness does not protect intentional personal misconduct.
Transfer-pricing manipulation and undocumented related-party payments

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may make a primary transfer-pricing adjustment, deny deductions, impose secondary adjustments, assess withholding tax, interest, and documentation penalties, and apply general tax penalties for resulting underpayment or inaccurate returns.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur liability for knowingly approving sham or unsupported transactions, including civil restitution and administrative sanctions. Criminal exposure may arise if the conduct forms part of tax fraud, accounting falsification, insolvency fraud, or money laundering.
False carbon accounting, greenwashing, or fraudulent environmental claims

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include tax reassessment, denial of deductions, commercial and consumer-protection sanctions, accounting liability, contractual damages, regulatory penalties, and criminal liability for fraud or document falsification where the elements are met.

Director personal liability: Directors and responsible officers may face civil compensation, director liability, professional consequences, and criminal prosecution for deliberate falsification or deceptive commercialization. Travel restrictions and imprisonment are not automatic and require the applicable judicial or statutory basis.
Withholding-tax failure and unlawful profit repatriation

Statutory sanction: The Spanish SL may be assessed for unwithheld tax, late-payment interest, surcharges, and withholding-related penalties. The underlying expense may also be denied and the payment recharacterized as a dividend or hidden profit distribution.

Director personal liability: Directors may be liable where they intentionally authorized non-compliant payments or failed to implement required controls. Personal liability can include civil claims, tax-collection liability in qualifying cases, and criminal exposure for deliberate tax fraud.
Money laundering, terrorist financing, or unlawful funds movement

Statutory sanction: Spanish anti-money-laundering breaches may attract substantial administrative fines, public or private sanctions, compliance restrictions, and reporting obligations. Money laundering is a criminal offense and may result in imprisonment, fines, confiscation, and corporate criminal liability.

Director personal liability: Directors, compliance officers, and beneficial owners may face personal criminal liability, asset freezing, confiscation, civil restitution, and judicial travel restrictions. Imprisonment depends on the offense and judicial determination.
Accounting falsification and corporate-record failure

Statutory sanction: Consequences may include tax adjustments, accounting and commercial sanctions, audit qualifications, civil damages, insolvency consequences, and criminal penalties for falsification or fraudulent accounting where statutory elements are satisfied.

Director personal liability: Directors may be personally liable for damages to the company, creditors, shareholders, and tax authorities. Criminal sanctions may include imprisonment, fines, disqualification, restitution, and confiscation.
Failure to file, pay, or respond to AEAT requirements

Statutory sanction: Late-filing surcharges, late-payment interest, fixed information-return penalties, percentage-based tax penalties, enforcement surcharges, account seizures, and other collection measures may apply.

Director personal liability: Directors may become secondarily liable where statutory derivation conditions are met, including deliberate non-compliance, cessation without payment, or obstruction of collection. Civil recovery and asset-preservation measures may follow.
Unlawful professional representation or assurance

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include professional, commercial, consumer-protection, contractual, and civil-liability sanctions; regulated audit violations may attract additional sanctions under Spanish audit legislation.

Director personal liability: Responsible directors and signatories may face personal civil damages, professional disqualification, administrative sanctions, and criminal exposure for fraud or unauthorized practice where applicable.
Shell-company and beneficial-ownership abuse

Statutory sanction: Possible outcomes include treaty-benefit denial, withholding-tax reassessment, transfer-pricing adjustments, general anti-avoidance application, tax penalties, beneficial-owner reporting consequences, and anti-money-laundering investigation.

Director personal liability: Directors and ultimate beneficial owners may face civil restitution, tax-collection liability, asset freezing, confiscation, judicial travel restrictions, and imprisonment where tax fraud, money laundering, or other criminal offenses are proven.
